archetype.name: Dual-Threat (pocket-first)
archetype.definition: A downfield passer who wins from the pocket with accuracy on throws of 10+ air yards, then turns broken plays into first downs with his legs rather than through designed runs.

report.headline: A brutal September hid the same downfield passer from last year's breakout
report.take:
Maye's 2025 season set the bar: 0.315 EPA per play (3rd), a 10.8 CPOE (3rd) and 14 wins. This year's full-season line, 0.209 EPA per dropback (12th) with 8 interceptions (43rd of 47), reads like a step back. That reading is wrong, or at least badly incomplete. The season splits into two parts. Against Seattle, Pittsburgh and Jacksonville, defenses that now rank 5th, 6th and 3rd, his passing EPA was negative every week, including a -14.2 in a 35-6 loss in Jacksonville. Over the five games since, against defenses ranked 12th to 31st, he has posted 0.45 EPA per dropback, a 10.2 CPOE, 14 touchdowns and only 2 of his 8 interceptions, and the Patriots went 4-1.

The engine is the ball traveling downfield. On throws of 10+ air yards he is at 0.61 EPA per attempt with a 12.5 CPOE. On 31 deep attempts he is at 0.892 per play with a 17.1 CPOE, and those deep throws account for more of his EPA total than his 105 short attempts do. Under 10 yards he is ordinary (0.097 per play), mostly because throws behind the line have cost the offense -22.4 EPA. That points to the screen game and a run game ranked 26th, not to Maye himself. When the pocket breaks down he runs: 26 scrambles at 0.767 EPA apiece with 16 first downs. That makes his 3.14-second time to throw a feature of how he plays, not a flaw.

What the numbers hide is a quiet change in how he plays. His aggressiveness, the share of throws into tight windows, has dropped from 17.9% to 12.39%. His pressure-to-sack rate has fallen to 22% (10th), after 40.5% and 35.6% in his first two years, and his bad-throw rate has improved to 10.3% (5th). He is holding the ball longer, waiting for throws to open and escaping instead of taking sacks. That is a real gain, not luck. The leaks are situational: third down (-0.113 EPA, 36.9% conversions), the red zone (50% completions, 3 picks) and under center (-0.288). With no run game to lean on, the field shrinks and his margin goes with it.

Where this goes depends on which half of the schedule is the truer test. The deep efficiency will come down, because 31 attempts is a hot sample, but his deep accuracy fits a passer who led the league in that area last year. The September interceptions came against top-six defenses, and some of the bad-throw spikes (16.7% against the Jets, 17.6% at Buffalo) came during the hot stretch. Expect a top-10 passer by efficiency who still gives away a few turnovers to defenses that can cover. The next opponent is one of those defenses.

strengths.title: Accuracy on throws beyond 10 yards
strengths.body: His intermediate and deep throws carry the offense, combining for 0.61 EPA per attempt with a 12.5 CPOE. Last year he ranked 3rd in CPOE, so his accuracy downfield is long-standing, not a sudden change. The deep EPA itself, on 31 attempts, will cool off, but his deep-ball accuracy should hold up.

strengths.title: Scrambles that pay for the pressure
strengths.body: He turns collapsing pockets into gains: 26 scrambles at 0.767 EPA each, with 16 of them moving the chains. Paired with a pressure-to-sack rate that has dropped into the league's top 10, his longer time to throw now buys him extra plays instead of costing him sacks. This reflects how he plays and should last.

strengths.title: Fewer bad throws than last year
strengths.body: His bad-throw rate has fallen to 10.3% (5th), down from last year's 13.2%, while his aggressiveness has dropped by about 5.5 points. He is taking fewer risks into tight windows and missing less. This supports the low interception rate of his last five games.

concerns.title: Interceptions arrive against good defenses
concerns.body: His 3.4% interception rate ranks 39th, and most of those picks came in a three-game stretch against defenses that now rank in the top six. The 1.3% rate over the last five games came against much weaker defenses. The truth sits somewhere in between, and the next opponent belongs to the tougher group.

concerns.title: Third down and red zone stall
concerns.body: He is below zero in EPA on both third down and in the red zone, completing half his red-zone throws with 3 interceptions. With the run game ranked 26th, the offense has nothing to lean on once the field shrinks, so this is partly his supporting cast. But the red-zone picks are his own.

concerns.title: Screens and under-center snaps drain value
concerns.body: Throws behind the line have produced -22.4 EPA with a -6.7 CPOE, and under-center dropbacks sit at -0.288 per play. Those are mostly scheme choices, not his failures, but they keep his short game around league average.

trend.note: Three straight weeks of negative passing EPA to open the season gave way to five straight positive games, peaking at 29.5 EPA against Las Vegas. The last three have been strong but a step below that peak, at 0.363 per dropback. The opponents in that run were mostly weak defenses, so read the rise with that in mind.

nextGame.headline: Packers take away explosives, and his tight end may be out
nextGame.body:
Green Bay is the first top-10 defense he has faced since September. The Packers rank 7th in EPA, allow the 2nd-lowest explosive pass rate and are 8th against deep throws. That aims directly at the part of his game producing most of his value. They have also held quarterbacks to the 5th-fewest PPR points. The way through is volume to wide receivers: offenses send them 64.6% of targets against Green Bay, above the league's 58%. The Packers also shut down tight ends harder than anyone (-5.1 PPR under average, 1st). New England is a 3-point home favorite with a 46.5 total, which projects a competitive game rather than a blowout.

Availability hurts him more than it helps. Hunter Henry (66% of snaps, 0.554 EPA per target, his second-best target) left the Miami game with a foot injury and is questionable, though this is the worst possible matchup for a tight end anyway. A.J. Brown is listed out with an ankle injury, and Vrabel would only say "we'll see" about practice. Brown's -0.23 EPA per target on 20 looks suggests his absence costs less than his name implies, but Mack Hollins could return from IR to add depth. TreVeyon Henderson is out with an illness, which leaves the backfield even thinner behind a run game ranked 26th. On the other side, Micah Parsons has not played this season, so his absence is already reflected in Green Bay's numbers, and linebacker Zaire Franklin (99% of snaps) is out. Green Bay's offense is missing two starting linemen, which could help New England's 6th-ranked sack rate shorten the Packers' drives.

keyMatchups.title: Deep ball versus a no-explosives defense
keyMatchups.body: His 0.892 deep EPA meets a defense ranked 2nd in explosive pass rate allowed and 8th on deep throws. If Green Bay keeps everything in front, he has to win underneath, where his EPA is close to average.

keyMatchups.title: DeMario Douglas against a WR-heavy funnel
keyMatchups.body: Douglas leads his targets at 0.666 EPA per target, and offenses send Green Bay well above the league share of throws to wide receivers. With Henry hurt and the tight end matchup closed off anyway, Douglas should be his main option.

keyMatchups.title: Scrambles against a missing linebacker
keyMatchups.body: With Franklin out of the middle of the defense, the scramble lanes that have produced 16 first downs could be more open. That matters most on third down, where he has struggled.

nextGame.watch: Whether he keeps taking shots downfield against a defense built to deny them, or settles for screens and checkdowns, which are his least productive throws.

restOfSeason.body:
The baseline is closer to last year's passer than to his September. His accuracy, his sack avoidance and his scrambling have all held up or improved, so the floor is a top-12 efficiency quarterback. The ceiling is the top-five level he reached in 2025 and over the last five games. What will regress is the deep-ball EPA on 31 attempts and the 9.1% touchdown rate of the hot stretch. The interception rate should land between his September and his October as the schedule mixes good and bad defenses.

Volume is steady at around 29 attempts a game in an offense that runs slightly more than expected, so expect his production to come from yards per attempt and touchdowns more than from raw volume. His rushing comes almost entirely from scrambles, which makes it reliable but modest. Designed runs have done nothing. The health of his receivers is the biggest unknown: an offense built around Douglas and Henry gets thin quickly if Henry misses time.
swingFactors: Hunter Henry's foot and A.J. Brown's ankle
How he handles top-10 defenses after his September struggles
Whether the run game rises from 26th to ease third downs and the red zone

confidence.note: The eight-game sample splits sharply by opponent quality, and his top receivers' health is uncertain.
